_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: This works out well according to the Rabbis: who disagree with Rabbi Yehuda [and say] that the fiftieth year is not part of the count of the Sabbatical cycles. It was necessary to count Jubilee Years, as you said.
rashi:a1.2: But according to Rabbi Yehuda, who says the fiftieth year: is the Jubilee Year and also counts toward the next Sabbatical cycle, why do I need to count Jubilee Years? Counting Sabbatical Years is enough: every seven years they would always observe a Sabbatical Year, since no year interrupts between them, and there is no room for error here.
rashi:a1.3: Certainly: what was taught above, that they counted Sabbatical and Jubilee Years in the days of Ezra, is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda.
rashi:a2.1: And did they not count Jubilee Years: from the days of Sennacherib [who exiled the tribes]?
rashi:a2.2: But isn’t it written: in the days of Zedekiah.
rashi:a3.1: “At the end of seven years you shall let go” etc., and we discussed it: “At the end of seven years” implies after seven years, so that the seventh year too [is served]; but isn’t it written, “and has served you six years”?
rashi:a3.2: Six for one who was sold: as it is written (Exodus 21:2): “Six years he shall serve.”
rashi:a3.3: And seven for one who was pierced: since the pierced slave does not go out until the Jubilee; and if he was pierced and the Jubilee fell in the eighth year from his piercing, he goes out in the Jubilee. Evidently there was a Jubilee in the days of Zedekiah, and Zedekiah lived at the time of the destruction of the Temple, many generations after the exile of Sennacherib.
rashi:a4.1: It is written in reproof: Jeremiah is rebuking them and saying to them: Did you send them free in those years when you were obligated to send them free?
rashi:a5.1: As it is written: in the days of Zedekiah, “For the seller shall not return to that which he has sold.” He was telling them: In the end you will be exiled, the Jubilee will be nullified, and fields will not return to their owners.
rashi:a5.2: Is it possible that the Jubilee had been nullified: from when the tribes of Reuben and Gad were exiled, and a prophet prophesies about it etc.?
rashi:a7.1: What connection does Josiah have with Bethel: the verse is written about Josiah when he was going about eradicating idol worship in the Land of Israel, and Bethel belonged to the kings of Israel. What business did Josiah, king of Judah, have there?
rashi:a7.2: Katzir [harvest]: [read it as] katzin, a ruler, for nun interchanges with resh, as it is written both Nebuchadnezzar and Nebuchadrezzar.
rashi:a8.1: Mishna. Houses of the courtyards: whose towns have no wall.
rashi:a8.2: Exceptional provisions: as it explains, they are redeemed immediately and need not wait two years in the buyer’s possession; and this is like houses of walled cities.
rashi:a8.3: And with a deduction of money: the buyer deducts for him according to the years they stayed in his possession, as with fields, as it is written (Leviticus 25:27): “Then let him count the years of its sale” etc.
rashi:a9.1: Gemara. “Shall be reckoned with the fields of the country”: this is written about houses of the courtyards.
rashi:a9.2: And with a deduction of money: if he comes to redeem them before the Jubilee.
rashi:a11.1: What is it saying: where would one get the idea that they do not go out in the Jubilee? They were juxtaposed to an ancestral field! So what was “and they shall go out in the Jubilee” needed for?
rashi:a11.2: And the Jubilee arrived in the second year: of the purchase by this one, who bought it from the treasurer.
rashi:a12.1: It belongs to the buyer [in perpetuity]: for so it was taught above: if another redeemed it from the Temple treasury, the Jubilee arrived and it was not redeemed, it is his in perpetuity.
rashi:a12.2: It goes out to the priests: for one who consecrates an ancestral field and another redeemed it, it goes out to the priests in the Jubilee. And that is why he specified the second year: had the Jubilee arrived in the first year, “and they shall go out in the Jubilee” would not be needed, for even if you compare it to houses of walled cities it has not yet become his in perpetuity, and it goes out in the Jubilee, since it has the exceptional provision of fields.
rashi:a13.1: Even if he did not redeem it: [if no] other [redeemed it], let it also leave the Temple treasury’s possession, since it is written “and they shall go out in the Jubilee,” which was not needed for an ordinary sale, since they were already juxtaposed to fields.
rashi:a14.1: A Levite, whose power is enhanced with regard to his sale: in that he redeems a field of the open land of their cities immediately, and their houses of walled cities they may redeem forever, and they go out in the Jubilee, as is stated below.
rashi:a14.2: His power is diminished with regard to his consecration: in that it does not go out without redemption, as is explained below.
rashi:a15.1: “That was sold…shall go out”: had it been written “And if a man purchases from the Levites, that was sold shall go out in the Jubilee,” without writing “house,” I would have said that even a Levite’s promissory notes and movable property, if he sold them, return to him in the Jubilee.
rashi:a17.1: And disagrees with Rabbi Oshaya: what Rav Huna said above, that if one consecrates a house among the houses of the courtyards and another redeemed it from the Temple treasury, it leaves his possession and returns to the owners in the Jubilee, disagrees with Rabbi Oshaya.
rashi:a17.2: Within “And he will give the money and it will be assured to him”: that whatever one buys from the Temple treasury, the purchase stands in his possession forever.
rashi:a18.1: When the verse specified: regarding one who redeems another’s ancestral field from the Temple treasury, that it leaves his possession and is divided [among the priests]: that is the one the Merciful One explicitly took out of the general rule of “and he will give the money and it will be assured to him.”
rashi:a18.2: But these: the houses of the courtyards stay as they are, within “it will be assured to him,” and do not leave the buyer’s possession.
rashi:a19.1: “And they shall go out in the Jubilee”: according to Rabbi Oshaya, why do I need it?
rashi:a20.1: It requires completion: to complete for him one year of the two years it is fit to remain in the buyer’s possession, as taught above at the beginning of our chapter: if he consumed it for one year before the Jubilee, they complete for him another year after the Jubilee.
rashi:a21.1: We read: “It is taught in accordance with Rav Huna.” In accordance with Rav Huna, who said above that if one consecrates a house among the houses of the courtyards and another redeemed it from the Temple [Rashi’s text reads “from the consecrator”], it goes out to the owners in the Jubilee.
rashi:a21.2: And a refutation of Rabbi Oshaya: who said they stay as they are, in the buyer’s possession.
rashi:a21.3: And he may redeem it always: even if another redeemed it, he redeems it from him; it is not like an ancestral field, about which it is written (Leviticus 27:20): “It shall not be redeemed any more.”
rashi:a21.4: If another redeemed it from the Temple treasury and the Jubilee arrived and it was not redeemed: by the consecrator from him, it returns to him for free.
tosafot:a5.1: But this teaches that Jeremiah brought them back and Josiah ruled over them: This is puzzling, for after Jeremiah brought them back they remained in the land before the destruction only thirty-six years, as I explained above in chapter 2 (Arakhin 12b). If so, they did not reach a Jubilee, so how can we account for “and they listened and let them go”? One can say that we can account for it with the slaves they had before they were exiled. And as for the Gemara’s question above, “But isn’t it written: And they listened and let them go,” the main force of the question is from what is written (Jeremiah 34:10): “And all the princes and all the people who entered into the covenant listened,” which implies that they entered into a covenant to send their slaves free in the Jubilee when the Jubilee arrived.
gershom:a1.1: This works out well according to the Rabbis: it was necessary to count Jubilee Years in order to sanctify the Sabbatical Year at its proper time.
gershom:a2.1: But according to Rabbi Yehuda, who says: that it counts for here and for there, for the Jubilee and to count from it one, two, three, four, up to seven.
gershom:a3.1: Why do I need: to count Jubilee Years? Counting Sabbatical Years is enough.
gershom:a4.1: That certainly: what was taught, that even on their arrival in the days of Ezra they counted Jubilee Years, is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, for according to Rabbi Yehuda it was not needed. [The Gemara goes on:] And did they not count Sabbatical and Jubilee Years after the tribe of Reuben and the tribe of Gad were exiled?
gershom:a5.1: And we discussed it: “At the end of seven years you shall let go”? It should have said “At the end of six years you shall let go,” at the end of six, which is “and has served you six years.”
gershom:a6.1: And Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said: six years for the one who was sold, as it is written, “If you buy a Hebrew slave, six years he shall serve,” and at the beginning of the seventh he goes free. And what it says, “At the end of seven years you shall let go,” is seven for the one who was pierced, for the law of a pierced slave is to serve until the Jubilee; and if he was pierced when seven years remained before the Jubilee, that is “at the end of seven years,” he goes out in the Jubilee. Evidently they also counted Jubilee Years after the tribes of Reuben and Gad were exiled.
gershom:a7.1: The tanna could say to you: what is written, “At the end of seven years you shall let go,” is written in reproof. The prophet says to them in astonishment, by way of reproof, “Did you send free?” That is to say: did you indeed fulfill “At the end of seven years you shall let go”?
gershom:a8.1: And was the Jubilee not in effect? But isn’t it written, “And they listened and let them go”? Evidently the Jubilee was in effect.
gershom:a9.1: Rather, Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Jeremiah brought them back: the tribes of Reuben and Gad, and Josiah ruled over them; therefore they counted Sabbatical and Jubilee Years.
gershom:a10.1: And from where do we derive that they returned? From the prophet’s prophecy, “For the seller shall not return to that which he has sold,” that is, that the Jubilee will again be nullified as at first, and fields will not return to their owners. Conclude from it that the tribes of Reuben and Gad returned: for if you should think they did not return, why would he need to prophesy that the Jubilee would be nullified? It had been nullified from the time the tribes of Reuben and Gad were exiled! Rather, conclude from it that they returned, and when they sinned he rebuked them and said it would be nullified.
gershom:a11.1: “And Josiah said: What monument is that” etc. And what connection does Josiah have with Bethel? Didn’t Bethel belong to the kings of Israel? Rather, conclude from it that Jeremiah brought them back and Josiah ruled over them.
gershom:a12.1: Set a harvest [katzir]: katzir is katzin, a ruler, for in many places nun interchanges with resh, as in Nebuchadnezzar and Nebuchadrezzar. Judah: that is Josiah, who at first was king over Judah.
gershom:a13.1: Houses of the courtyards: these are villages that have no wall.
gershom:a14.1: One accords them the exceptional provisions of houses of walled cities and the exceptional provisions of fields. How so? They are redeemed immediately after they were sold, and they are redeemed throughout the twelve months, like houses; and that is the exceptional provision of houses of walled cities.
gershom:a15.1: With a deduction of money: he deducts for him the value of the years in which he consumed the produce.
gershom:a16.1: And they go out in the Jubilee [if they were not redeemed]: that is, they do not become the buyer’s in perpetuity; and when they are redeemed, they are redeemed with a deduction of money, by the law of fields. Yet they are not like fields, for a field one may redeem only after two years, and these are redeemed [even] immediately.
gershom:a17.1: The verse states: “They may be redeemed,” immediately: like the law of houses of walled cities.
gershom:a18.1: [One might have thought that they do not go out in the Jubilee.] What is it saying? On the contrary: since their power is enhanced, their law is that they go out in the Jubilee.
gershom:a19.1: And the Jubilee arrived in the second year: after he redeemed it.
gershom:a20.1: To what will you compare it: this house.
gershom:a21.1: If you compare it to houses of walled cities, it becomes the buyer’s in perpetuity: this one who redeemed it from the Temple treasury, for it became his in perpetuity after twelve months, as we said above: if another redeemed it from the Temple treasury and the twelve months came to an end and it was not redeemed, it is his in perpetuity.
gershom:a22.1: And if you compare it to an ancestral field, it goes out to the priests: since another redeemed it, as we say in the previous chapter: if the treasurer sold it to another, it is not redeemed, but goes out to the priests, as it is written: “But the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee…shall be for the priest.”
gershom:a23.1: For this reason it was necessary, “and they shall go out in the Jubilee”: that it returns to the owners.
gershom:a24.1: Even if another did not redeem it: if they consecrated it, it should also go out to the owners, since it is written “and they shall go out in the Jubilee.”
gershom:a25.1: Abaye said to him: if another did not redeem it, it does not go out to him. [It is] a decree, so that people will not say [consecrated property goes out without redemption].
gershom:a26.1: And from where do we derive: that it does not go out without redemption? From a Levite, [whose power is enhanced with regard to his sale, as we learn below: the priests and the Levites sell always and redeem always; his power is diminished with regard to his consecration, as we say below that it does not go out without redemption. An Israelite, whose power is diminished with regard to his sale, in that he redeems only after two years.]
gershom:a27.1: And there, from where do we derive: that a Levite’s consecrated property does not go out without redemption?
gershom:a28.1: As it is taught: “And if a man purchases [from the Levites], the house that was sold in the city of his possession shall go out in the Jubilee.”
gershom:a29.1: [I would understand: that even if he sold his slaves, his promissory notes and his movable property, they return in the Jubilee.]
gershom:a30.1: The verse states: “House…in the city [of his possession],” which are land, to exclude these.
gershom:a31.1: If so, what does the verse teach by “that was sold,” which implies any sale? It wrote “that was sold” for this: his sale [of land] goes out [for free] in the Jubilee, [but his consecration does not] go out for free, only with redemption; and all the more so an Israelite’s consecration does not leave the Temple treasury without redemption. [The text carries an older bracketed reading of the middle phrase.]
gershom:a32.1: [And what Rav Huna says, that if one consecrates a house among the houses of unwalled courtyards and another redeemed it from the Temple treasury, it leaves his possession in the Jubilee and returns to the owners, this disagrees with Rabbi Oshaya, for Rabbi Oshaya said:] All were included in “And he will give the money and it will be assured to him”: whether one consecrates his house or his ancestral field, or a house among the houses of walled cities or among the houses of courtyards, it belongs to the redeemer and does not leave his possession in the Jubilee.
gershom:a33.1: [When the verse specified: regarding one who redeems an ancestral field from the Temple treasury, “But the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee…shall be for the priest”: it is a field that another redeems and it goes out to the priests in the Jubilee.]
gershom:a34.1: But all these: one who redeems houses of courtyards from the Temple treasury.
gershom:a35.1: Stay as they are: it does not leave his possession in the Jubilee. And this is the dispute with Rav Huna.
gershom:a36.1: [But according to Rabbi Oshaya, why do I need “and they shall go out in the Jubilee” of houses of courtyards?]
gershom:a37.1: “And they shall go out in the Jubilee” is needed only for one who sells a house among the houses of courtyards, and the Jubilee arrived etc. [If you compare it to an ancestral field,] it requires completion: [as taught at the beginning of our chapter: if he consumed it for one year before the Jubilee, they complete for him another year after the Jubilee.] It might enter your mind that it does not go out in the Jubilee but that they complete the year for him; therefore “and they shall go out in the Jubilee” was needed, [to teach] that they do not complete it for him.
gershom:a38.1: [It is taught] in accordance with Rav Huna: as he said, if another redeemed it from the Temple treasury, the Jubilee arrived and it was not redeemed, it returns to the owners in the Jubilee. This is the refutation of Rabbi Oshaya, for he says, “but these stay as they are,” that they do not return in the Jubilee.
rashi:b1.1: Mishna. Two courtyards: a town that has only two courtyards.
rashi:b2.1: Gemara. Do I not know that they have no wall: for “houses of the courtyards” implies that it is not a town but a settlement of adjacent courtyards.
rashi:b2.2: Like those that have no wall: since it does not amount to a town.
rashi:b2.3: And how many: are they, that their wall should not be counted as that of a walled town? Two courtyards etc.
rashi:b3.1: Say a house and a courtyard, a house and a courtyard: but if there are two houses in each courtyard, they are like a walled city and not like the houses of the courtyards.
rashi:b3.2: If so, let it write “courtyards”: and not write “houses,” and I would know that there is no courtyard without a house.
rashi:b4.1: Mishna. An Israelite who inherited: houses of a walled city from his mother’s father, a Levite, does not redeem according to this procedure, that if he sold it, it becomes the buyer’s in perpetuity at the end of a year; rather, he may always redeem it, like a Levite, as it is written about them (Leviticus 25:32): “The Levites shall have a perpetual right of redemption.”
rashi:b5.1: Unless he is: the seller is a Levite; to exclude an Israelite who inherited from his mother’s father, a Levite, who does not redeem like a Levite.
rashi:b5.2: And the cities of the Levites: of the cities given to the Levites in the days of Joshua; to exclude a Levite who inherited from his mother’s father, an Israelite, who does not redeem like a Levite. And now the first clause [of the mishna] contradicts the last, and the Gemara resolves it.
rashi:b5.3: These matters are not: [the matters of] a perpetual right of redemption are stated only regarding the cities of the Levites, but we do not require that he be a Levite. With an Israelite who inherited from his mother’s father, a Levite, the Rabbis concede that he redeems like a Levite, since this is of the cities of the Levites; but with a Levite who inherited from his mother’s father, an Israelite, the Rabbis concede that he does not redeem like a Levite, for the Merciful One made it depend on the cities of the Levites.
rashi:b7.1: Gemara. And it asks: “He does not redeem according to this procedure” of an Israelite; rather, like whom? Like a Levite? [Asked in astonishment.] But the last clause teaches, “unless he is a Levite” etc.
rashi:b8.1: Granted, the cities of the Levites: we require, to exclude a Levite who inherited from an Israelite, as it is written: “the cities of the Levites.”
rashi:b8.2: But a Levite, from where do we derive: that we require that he be a Levite, to exclude an Israelite who inherited from his mother’s father, a Levite?
rashi:b8.3: “And if a man purchases from the Levites”: which implies, to some of the Levites I gave permission to redeem, and not to all of them.
rashi:b9.1: And it is taught: that we expound it this way. This is how we read it in Torat Kohanim: “From the Levites,” what does it teach? For one might have thought a Levite may redeem from an Israelite. That is, had it written only “The Levites shall have a perpetual right of redemption,” I could say that a Levite who sold to an Israelite may redeem it forever, since the Israelite’s power is diminished with regard to his sale, in that [his house] becomes [the buyer’s] in perpetuity at the end of a year.
rashi:b9.2: And this one’s power is enhanced: as it is written, “a perpetual right of redemption” etc. But a Levite who sold to a Levite may not redeem; rather, it would become [the buyer’s] in perpetuity at the end of a year.
rashi:b9.3: The verse states: “From the Levites”: to exclude a Levite born of a mamzeret or of a Gibeonite woman; and all the more so an Israelite who inherited from his mother’s father, a Levite, for he is a full Israelite.
rashi:b12.1: Mishna. A field, a migrash [empty lot]: the migrash is a thousand cubits around the city, from what is written (Numbers 35:4–5): “From the wall of the city and outward a thousand cubits round about.” Beyond that thousand, the Levites had a thousand cubits for fields and vineyards, as it is written: “And you shall measure from outside the city” etc. Take a thousand cubits of migrash from them, and the rest is fields and vineyards. The migrash is empty of everything: there is no house in it and it is not sown; it is a beautification for the city.
rashi:b12.2: One may not render a field a migrash: because of the settlement of the Land of Israel; that would be destruction, since it reduces the sowing.
rashi:b12.3: Nor a migrash a field: since he destroys the beauty of the city.
rashi:b12.4: A migrash one may not make into a city: that they would build houses in it, for a city is not beautiful without a migrash; and all the more so one may not make a city into a migrash, for one does not destroy the settlement of the city.
rashi:b13.1: Sell always: even in the Jubilee Year itself; so I heard. But it is difficult for me: why? Just as Rav and Shmuel disagree at the beginning of the chapter (Arakhin 29b) about an Israelite who sold his field in the Jubilee Year itself, so too one could disagree here, and say an a fortiori argument: if what was already sold goes out now, [all the more so what is sold now], for we said above (Arakhin 28a) that a Levite’s sale returns in the Jubilee Year. And it seems to me that since the other chapter taught “they consecrate always and redeem always,” it taught [“sell always”] here too.
rashi:b13.2: Redeem always: for their houses of walled cities do not become [the buyer’s] in perpetuity.
rashi:b16.1: Gemara. One might have thought that also this one: a Levite, is so: that if he sold his ancestral field, those thousand cubits beyond the migrash, he would not be permitted to redeem it in less than two years.
rashi:b17.1: Since it is stated: about one who consecrates an ancestral field and another redeemed it from the Temple treasury, that in the Jubilee Year it goes out to the priests, as it is written: “But the field” etc.
rashi:b17.2: One might have thought that also: a Levite is so, that if he consecrated a field and did not redeem it, he would lose it in the Jubilee. The verse states: “a perpetual right of redemption” etc.
rashi:b19.1: These cities: those given to the Levites.
rashi:b19.2: One does not make them small villages: since they are cities of refuge, and there must be a settlement there to serve as a refuge for killers.
rashi:b19.3: Nor large cities: since people gather there from everywhere for commerce, and the blood redeemer would often be found there, lie in wait for the killer and kill him.
rashi:b19.4: Rather, intermediate towns: without a wall.
rashi:b20.1: Here, where it was surrounded and ultimately settled: you will not find that with the Levites, as you said. But settled and ultimately surrounded you will find with them, for after the cities were given to them in the days of Joshua, they surrounded them [with a wall].
rashi:b21.1: And in a case like this: settled and ultimately surrounded, is it a wall? A verse was needed to exclude it!
rashi:b21.2: A dwelling house in a walled city: a house that was settled and built in a walled city, which implies that it was surrounded and ultimately settled.
rashi:b22.1: One might have thought even if Jews surrounded it: after they conquered the land, and even before they settled in it.
rashi:b22.2: And it is stated below “wall”: (Deuteronomy 3:5) “All these were fortified cities” etc.
rashi:b23.1: After that: after the Jews conquered them.
rashi:b24.1: Rav Sala interpreted it [Rashi’s heading names Rav Sala; the daf reads Rav Yosef, son of Rav Sala Ḥasida]: Actually, where it was surrounded and ultimately settled; and as for what is difficult for you, “these cities one does not make” etc.
rashi:b24.2: For example, where they fell to them: by lottery, in the days of Joshua.
gershom:b1.1: And these are the houses of the courtyards: that have this law.
gershom:b2.1: Two courtyards of [two] houses each, even though they are surrounded [by a wall]: their law is like houses of the courtyards, like villages that have no wall; but fewer than this, they are not like houses of the courtyards. [A gloss in the printed edition: it seems the tanna means to exclude more than this, which would not be like houses of courtyards; perhaps this is a scribal error and it should read “but more than this.” This requires study.]
gershom:b3.1: Houses of the courtyards: implies villages that have no wall.
gershom:b4.1: [What does the verse teach by “which have no wall”? That even though they have a wall surrounding them from the days of Joshua, they are as if they have no wall, for they are not under the law of houses of walled cities.]
gershom:b5.1: And say a house and a courtyard, a house and a courtyard: that is, two houses and two courtyards, and not that there be two houses in each courtyard.
gershom:b6.1: If so: that there is only one house in each courtyard.
gershom:b7.1: Let it write: “courtyards,” and there would be no need to write “houses,” for an ordinary courtyard is not without one house.
gershom:b8.1: No: a courtyard that has no house is not called a courtyard but a karpef [enclosure]. And since it was necessary to write “houses” and “courtyards,” conclude from it: two courtyards of two houses each.
gershom:b9.1: [An Israelite who inherited from his mother’s father, a Levite,] does not redeem according to this procedure: like other Israelites who inherit from their Israelite relatives (but his law is like a Levite’s, and likewise a Levite etc.). [For the Levites are not under the law of one who sells an ancestral field for two years, nor under the law of houses of walled cities that become the buyer’s in perpetuity, nor likewise under the law of courtyards, as it is stated: “as the houses of the cities of the Levites are their possession,” unless he is a Levite and in the cities of the Levites. It now implies that both an Israelite who inherited from his mother’s father, a Levite, and a Levite who inherited from his mother’s father, an Israelite, redeem under the law of an Israelite, and never redeem by the order of a Levite, who sells always and redeems always, unless he is a Levite and in the cities of the Levites.]
gershom:b10.1: And the Rabbis say: These matters are stated only in the cities of the Levites: [this implies] that the Rabbis hold that even an Israelite who inherited in the cities of the Levites sells and redeems by the law of the Levites, for the Merciful One made it depend on the cities of the Levites. And in this they disagree: we do not say “unless he is a Levite.”
gershom:b11.1: [Rather, like whom? Like a Levite? But it teaches “unless he is a Levite and the cities of the Levites,” that is, one who is a Levite and in the cities of the Levites redeems by the law of a Levite, and not an Israelite in the cities of the Levites, [that he should] redeem like a Levite.] Rather, say: he redeems only according to this procedure: that we said above, by the law of an Israelite in the cities of Israel.
gershom:b12.1: Granted, the cities of the Levites: we find that they have a perpetual right of redemption and nothing else, as it is written, “as the houses of the cities of the Levites are their possession.” But from where do we derive that a Levite in the cities of the Levites has this law, and no other person?
gershom:b13.1: As it is written: “And if a man purchases from the Levites”: that is, a Levite who sold his field to an Israelite may redeem it forever.
gershom:b14.1: [One might have thought a Levite may redeem from an Israelite: forever.]
gershom:b15.1: As this one: the Levite, his power is enhanced with regard to his sale, as explained above.
gershom:b16.1: But a Levite: who sold to a Levite, since the power of both is enhanced, may not redeem.
gershom:b17.1: The verse states: “From the Levites”: that even a Levite may redeem from a Levite.
gershom:b18.1: “From the Levites,” and not all the Levites: “from the Levites” implies an exclusion, that is, there are Levites who are not under this law of redemption, namely a Levite who is a Gibeonite and a Levite who is a mamzer.
gershom:b19.1: (Unless he is a Levite, we do not say: for we do not require both.) [But “unless he is a Levite and the cities of the Levites” we do not say, for we do not require both.]
gershom:b20.1: Sell always: even in the Jubilee Year itself.
gershom:b21.1: And redeem always: even immediately, as soon as he sold.
gershom:b22.1: Shall not change: from what it is.
gershom:b23.1: And since it is stated: “Holy unto the Lord, as a field dedicated; his ancestral field shall be for the priest.”
gershom:b24.1: One might have thought that also this one is so: that a Levite who consecrated his field, it goes out to the priests in the Jubilee.
gershom:b25.1: These cities: of the Levites, about which it is written (Numbers 35:6): “And to them you shall add forty-two cities.”
gershom:b26.1: Small forts [tirim]: like towers. [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text reads tirim, forts, where the printed Gemara reads kefarim, villages.]
gershom:b27.1: Rather, intermediate towns: that are not surrounded by a wall. Evidently they have no houses of walled cities.
gershom:b28.1: It is not difficult: here, where it was surrounded by a wall and ultimately settled, and they gave it to the Levites, they do not have [the law of] houses of walled cities, for they break down their walls and make them intermediate towns. [A gloss in the printed edition suggests the reading: “the Levites do not have it; rather, they would break down their walls” etc.]
gershom:b29.1: Here, where it was settled: without a wall, and they gave it to the Levites.
gershom:b30.1: And ultimately surrounded: the Levites surrounded it after it was theirs; they have the (law of) houses of walled cities.
gershom:b31.1: A dwelling house in a walled city: it must be a walled city before there is a dwelling [house] in it.
gershom:b32.1: One might have thought even if Jews surrounded it: with a wall and afterward settled it, it would have the law of houses of walled cities.
gershom:b33.1: And it is stated below “wall”: “All these were fortified cities, with high walls.”
gershom:b34.1: Just as below: gentiles surrounded them with a wall.
gershom:b35.1: So too here: with houses of walled cities, gentiles surrounded them with a wall beforehand, that is, before Israel inherited the land.
gershom:b36.1: Rav Yosef interpreted it: that is, in a case like this they can have houses of walled cities.
gershom:b37.1: Where they fell to them: walled cities, by inheritance from a mother’s father who was an Israelite. [Rashi reads it as falling to them by lottery in the days of Joshua.]
gershom:b38.1: One may not render a field a migrash: those thousand cubits around the city, which are open space for the city’s beauty, one may not make into a field, for they are not sown; and a field that is for sowing one may not make into a migrash.
gershom:b39.1: In what case is this statement said? In the cities of the Levites: as it says in the Gemara, “shall not change.”
gershom:b40.1: Nor a city a migrash, so that they will not destroy the cities of Israel: one may not destroy a city that is settled to make it a migrash, empty open space, so that one will not change it from what it is.
